messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani was forty-three when her younger brother was killed by a drunk driver who ran a red light at three in the afternoon. He was a schoolteacher, on his way to pick up his daughter. That was the snapshot that stayed: the phone call from her sister-in-law, the drive to the hospital, the moment the doctor said the words she already knew. She could still hear the sound of her own scream in the waiting room, and the fluorescent lights humming above her. What her mind held onto was not a story but a few frozen pictures—the doctor's face, the linoleum floor, her sister-in-law's hand gripping the armrest.

In the months that followed, Leilani found herself unable to make sense of it. She had spent her career as a forensic analyst examining evidence, finding patterns, building cases on facts that held together. But this death had no pattern, no meaning, no higher purpose she could trace. She had lost her faith—in the idea that the world was orderly, in the notion that being careful or good or smart could protect someone. She kept telling herself that her life had been destroyed, and the more she said it, the more she believed it. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. Not her work, not the meals her husband made, not the sun setting over the bay she had always loved.

Because she believed that nothing mattered, she began to act as though nothing mattered. She stopped going into the office. She told herself she would catch up on reports from home, but she rarely opened her laptop. At night she stayed up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through news articles about car accidents, reading the comments, searching for something she could not name. Days blurred into nights. She forgot to eat. Her husband would find her at the kitchen table at midnight staring at a cold cup of tea, and she would say she was not hungry. She had come to believe that feeding herself felt like an act of pretending—pretending that she was still living a life worth sustaining.

Her belief that everything good was behind her made each memory hit harder. When the snapshots came—the doctor's face, the linoleum floor—they did not just bring back the event; they confirmed that the world was empty now. She had lost faith, and the memories were proof of what she had lost. The auditory recall was the worst: sometimes she would hear her brother say her name, exactly the way he used to, and the sound was so vivid and so painful that she would press her palms against her ears until the pressure hurt. When the memory returned she felt so overwhelmed by emotion that she had to stop whatever she was doing—not that she was doing much.

Her avoidance, however, only tightened the grip of those moments. The less she engaged with the world, the more those snapshot memories intruded. Going to work had once anchored her, provided structure; without it, the memories had more room, not less. And the more she avoided, the more she became convinced that her life was hollow. Each day she did not go to work confirmed that she no longer had a purpose. Each night she stayed awake reinforced the idea that she was not living anyway, so why bother with sleep? The cycle fed itself: she avoided because she believed her life was destroyed, and the avoidance proved her right. She had come to see herself as someone who existed in the aftermath of her own life, a person who had been a forensic analyst, a sister, a wife, but was no longer sure she was any of those things.

It was her husband who finally convinced her to seek help, not because she wanted to, but because she noticed that she had stopped disagreeing with him. When he said she was disappearing, she did not argue. What frightened her most was not the sadness—it was the flatness. The feeling that even the sadness was fading into something emptier. She came to therapy because she was afraid that if she did not, she would stop feeling anything at all.
